strengths: The paper identifies a real evaluation bottleneck for algorithm discovery agents and proposes a coherent benchmark/generator design with explicit meta-train/meta-test separation, editable modules, multiple domains, multiple evaluation types, and mechanisms to reduce evaluation hacking by rebuilding non-editable files at meta-test time.

The engineering contribution appears substantial: DiscoGen covers 10 analyzed domains and hundreds of millions of combinatorial configurations, with detailed appendices describing domains, prompts, task splits, task-count derivations, hyperparameters, compute, and per-task results. The claimed open-source release would make the contribution practically useful if complete.

The evaluation is broader than many agent benchmark papers: it evaluates three open-source LLM-based ADAs, reports success rates and Elo-style comparisons, includes an all-fixed baseline, studies single-module versus all-module tasks, provides success@3 and per-task breakdowns, and includes a prompt-optimization case study demonstrating one plausible use of procedural tasks.

The discussion of limitations, contamination, safety, labor impact, compute cost, and future private API evaluation is unusually detailed and appropriate. The paper does not hide that current ADAs often fail or underperform baselines, which strengthens the credibility of the benchmark motivation.

The presentation is generally clear despite the paper's length. The terminology around inner-loop, meta-loop, ADA optimization, and ADA evaluation is helpful, and the appendices make many implementation details inspectable.
weaknesses: The central claim that DiscoGen provides millions of meaningful, diverse algorithm-discovery tasks is only partially supported. The task-count argument is largely combinatorial over datasets, modules, backends, initializations, and evaluation types; this may substantially overstate effective diversity because many tasks share the same codebase, datasets, metrics, and algorithmic structure, and some combinations may be near-duplicates or low-value variants.

The empirical validation of diversity and usefulness is suggestive but not definitive. Rank correlations and per-task plots show variation, but they are based on a small set of ADAs and DiscoBench tasks, not on broad sampling from the full generator. There is limited evidence that randomly sampled tasks are consistently well-calibrated, non-degenerate, or useful for training ADAs at scale.

The DiscoBench evaluation methodology has several ad hoc choices that affect conclusions: Elo aggregation across heterogeneous metrics, a custom failure penalty, only three meta-seeds, 100 bootstrap rounds, omission of hard tasks in the until-success analysis, and very wide confidence intervals in some DiscoBench All results. These choices are reasonable starting points but not yet fully validated as a principled benchmark scoring protocol.

The prompt-optimization case study is interesting but limited: it uses one ADA backbone, one prompt optimizer model, 30 optimization steps, and a small number of task-diversity settings. The monotonic meta-test trend is promising, but it is not enough to establish that DiscoGen enables robust ADA optimization more generally.

The comparison to existing benchmarks is mostly conceptual rather than empirical. The paper argues that MLE-Bench, MLGymBench, and related suites have structural flaws, but does not run controlled comparisons showing that DiscoGen scores better predict future ADA performance, reduce contamination effects in practice, or produce more reliable rankings.

Reproducibility is promising but still somewhat underspecified in the manuscript itself. It claims open-source release and provides many prompts and hyperparameters, but the reviewable PDF does not expose a repository link, exact model serving details, seeds, dataset preprocessing hashes, or complete instructions sufficient to independently reproduce the full 23,000 GPU-hour evaluation. Some domains depend on external datasets and APIs, which may complicate replication.

The paper would benefit from a more explicit limitations section separating benchmark limitations from broader impact. Important caveats such as inflated task counts, task-quality validation, private benchmark maintenance, and dependence on expensive compute are present but spread across the text rather than crisply tied to the main claims.

strengths: The paper targets a timely problem: how to evaluate and improve algorithm-discovery agents without relying on small, saturated, potentially contaminated task suites. The meta-train/meta-test distinction is a useful design choice and directly addresses a real weakness in existing benchmarks.

DiscoGen's modular task formulation is practically appealing. Separating editable modules from fixed code and regenerating meta-test code after the agent finishes are sensible mechanisms for reducing evaluation hacking and for probing different kinds of algorithmic changes.

The manuscript is broad in scope, with ten implemented domains, a fixed DiscoBench evaluation suite, appendices documenting task prompts/splits, and compute/cost details. The rank-correlation and module-combination analyses are reasonable first attempts to test task diversity and difficulty.
The paper includes a thoughtful impact discussion covering safety, misuse, labor displacement, compute costs, and the risks of optimizing automated research agents.
weaknesses: The main contribution is more infrastructure proposal than demonstrated scientific advance. The paper repeatedly claims that DiscoGen enables millions of meaningful algorithm-discovery tasks, but the count is largely combinatorial over datasets/modules/backends and does not establish that most generated tasks are well-posed, non-redundant, solvable, or useful for training/evaluating ADAs.

The empirical validation is weak relative to the scale of the claims. DiscoBench experiments show that current agents often fail or underperform the all-fixed baseline, especially in DiscoBench All; this demonstrates difficulty, but only weakly supports the claim that the benchmark provides reliable signal for discovering better algorithms.

The prompt-optimization case study is not convincing enough to substantiate the broader optimization-loop story. It uses one ADA/model setting, a small number of optimization conditions, noisy Elo-style evaluation, and no strong baselines such as random prompt search, human prompt tuning, repeated prompt-optimizer seeds, or compute-matched alternatives.

The evaluation methodology has unresolved issues. Elo aggregation over heterogeneous tasks and datasets can obscure absolute performance and failure modes, the failure penalty is somewhat ad hoc, and many conclusions rely on small numbers of meta-seeds. The paper would be stronger with clearer per-domain statistical tests and explicit sensitivity analyses for the aggregation scheme.

The benchmark design may bias agents toward engineering around templates rather than genuine algorithm discovery. Although the authors try to avoid full-codebase modification, many tasks still appear to measure whether an agent can produce valid code under narrow interfaces and budgets, and the paper does not sufficiently separate implementation robustness from algorithmic novelty.

Originality is moderate. Applying procedural generation to algorithm-discovery tasks is interesting, but many ingredients are natural combinations of existing benchmark, AutoML/meta-learning, and PCG ideas. The paper does not provide a deep new algorithmic method or a particularly rigorous theory of what makes a generated discovery task valid.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The appendices provide useful details, but reproducing the headline results appears expensive, dependent on API-served models, and sensitive to agent/tooling details. The manuscript states DiscoGen is open-source, but the reviewable evidence in the paper is insufficient to verify ease of reproduction or long-term benchmark stability.

Some claims are overstated. Statements that DiscoGen overcomes contamination, supports open-ended learning, or enables safe specialist superhuman agents are framed too strongly compared with the evidence. The authors themselves acknowledge that public DiscoBench will become contaminated and that a private API suite is only future work.

strengths: The paper identifies a real bottleneck for algorithm discovery agents: existing benchmarks are small, fixed, prone to contamination, and often conflate research skill with software engineering. The DiscoGen framing of meta-train/meta-test task generation is well motivated and addresses an important evaluation gap.

The proposed resource is substantial. DiscoGen covers 10 evaluated domains across supervised learning, RL, language modeling, Bayesian optimization, continual learning, unlearning, and other settings, with modular editable components, held-out datasets, multiple initialization modes, and explicit task-count derivations.

DiscoBench is a useful companion benchmark. The paper gives concrete evaluation protocols, fixed task splits, baselines, success rates, Elo-style aggregate results, per-task appendix results, and analysis showing that current ADAs often fail to robustly implement even standard algorithms.

The empirical evidence supports the main utility claim: generated tasks provide signal for comparing ADAs, task difficulty increases with editable-module complexity, and prompt optimization over more generated tasks improves DiscoBench performance in the presented case study.

Reproducibility is comparatively strong for this type of systems paper: the authors state the code is open-source, document task domains, datasets, prompts, hyperparameters, Elo computation, compute costs, and provide extensive appendices with task descriptions and per-task results.

The paper treats limitations and ethics more seriously than many benchmark papers. It discusses contamination, future private evaluation, compute/environmental costs, misuse risks of automated algorithm discovery, and the need for human-in-the-loop scoping.
weaknesses: The strongest claims about diversity and low redundancy are only partially established. The combinatorial task count is impressive, but many generated configurations may be closely related; the main quantitative diversity evidence is based on DiscoBench rank correlations from a small set of models/baselines rather than broad semantic or human validation of the full generator distribution.

The experimental evaluation is still narrow relative to the scope of the benchmark. Most results use one agent scaffold, three open-source LLMs, and three meta-seeds; the paper does not evaluate stronger closed-source ADAs on DiscoBench, non-LLM search methods, or training/optimization of ADA weights, despite positioning DiscoGen as infrastructure for these directions.

The prompt-optimization case study is promising but not decisive. It appears to have limited replication, uses changing sampled tasks across conditions, and reports aggregate Elo improvements without enough controls to fully separate task diversity from stochasticity, prompt-optimizer behavior, or sampled-domain difficulty.

The public DiscoBench contamination issue remains unresolved. The proposed private API benchmark is future work, so the released benchmark may inherit the same long-term leakage risks that motivate the paper, even if current experiments avoid them.

The Elo aggregation and failure penalty are somewhat hard to interpret. Penalizing invalid solutions is sensible, but the resulting scores mix implementation robustness and algorithm quality, and the paper could provide clearer raw-score summaries and sensitivity analyses for the rating procedure.

Some claims are overstated. For example, saying expansion to other evaluation types is “trivial” and that adding domains requires only mild adaptation underplays the engineering and validation burden, especially for complex ML domains with expensive inner loops.

The paper is long and appendix-heavy. The presentation is generally clear, but key evidence for diversity, reproducibility, task solvability, and prompt optimization is scattered across many appendices, making the main argument harder to audit.

strengths: The paper targets an important bottleneck for algorithm discovery agents: current benchmarks are small, fixed, contamination-prone, and often lack a proper meta-train/meta-test distinction. The motivation is compelling and well connected to procedural generation in RL.

DiscoGen is a useful and ambitious benchmark/generator design. The modular task definition, editable modules, meta-train/meta-test separation, alternative initializations, and support for many ML domains make the framework potentially valuable beyond the specific experiments in the paper.

The manuscript provides substantial implementation and experimental detail, including task-domain descriptions, DiscoBench splits, prompts, Elo calculation, compute/cost estimates, per-task results, success@3, and until-success analyses. This is stronger reproducibility documentation than many benchmark papers, assuming the promised open-source release is complete.

The empirical results demonstrate several useful properties: existing ADAs fail often even on implementable baselines, all-edit tasks are harder than single-edit tasks, baseline initialization is easier than empty initialization, and meta-test evaluation can differ materially from meta-train evaluation.

The limitations and impact discussion are unusually explicit about contamination, compute cost, misuse, human-in-the-loop constraints, and the need for a private evaluation API. I would not penalize the paper for acknowledging these issues.
weaknesses: The central scale claim is partly overstated. The “~100B tasks” count is combinatorial over dataset subsets, module choices, backends, initialization, and evaluation type, but the paper only validates a tiny curated subset and one larger module sweep. This does not establish that the full generated space consists of meaningful, non-redundant, well-calibrated tasks.

The empirical support for DiscoGen as an optimization environment is limited. The prompt-optimization study appears to use one optimization trajectory per Ktasks setting, with changing sampled tasks and a stochastic Claude-based optimizer. Many confidence intervals overlap, and the monotonic/generalization claims are stronger than the evidence warrants.

DiscoBench is not yet public and the paper proposes a private API with undisclosed datasets. This may be practically necessary for contamination resistance, but it weakens independent reproducibility of the headline evaluation unless the API, fixed splits, scoring, and versioning are available at review time.

The evaluation is narrow relative to the ambition: all main ADA results use the MLGym scaffold with three open-source LLMs, and there is no direct empirical comparison against existing ADA benchmarks beyond a property table and discussion. This makes it hard to know whether DiscoBench rankings are stable across agent architectures or whether DiscoGen improves development more than simpler curated task expansion.

The Elo aggregation and failure penalty are somewhat ad hoc and can obscure absolute task performance. The paper reports success rates and per-task plots, which helps, but the main tables depend heavily on this comparative scoring pipeline and would benefit from stronger justification and sensitivity analysis.

Some claims about contamination resistance, semantic diversity, and safety are plausible but not fully demonstrated. Procedural generation reduces certain leakage risks, yet many datasets and base codebases are public, and the impact discussion’s claim that scoped specialist optimization is safer remains mostly conceptual.

Presentation is generally clear, but the paper is very long and mixes a concrete benchmark contribution with many speculative future research directions. The main contribution would be sharper if the core validation of generated-task quality, reproducibility, and benchmark reliability were foregrounded more than the promissory sections.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely bottleneck: evaluating and improving algorithm-discovery agents requires more than a small fixed set of hand-written tasks. The meta-train/meta-test framing for discovered algorithms is conceptually sound and is a useful correction to several existing benchmark designs.

DiscoGen's modular task construction is a plausible and practically useful benchmark/platform contribution. The paper covers a broad set of domains, editable algorithm components, initialization choices, and evaluation modes, and the appendix gives substantial implementation detail about task domains, splits, agent budgets, Elo aggregation, and compute cost.

The DiscoBench experiments reveal meaningful failure modes of current ADAs: low success rates, syntax failures, hard-coded/meta-train-overfit solutions, and frequent underperformance relative to fixed baselines. These negative findings are useful and honestly reported.

The paper includes a thoughtful impact discussion covering misuse, labor, accessibility, environmental cost, and scoped human-in-the-loop algorithm discovery. The limitations around contamination, compute, and incomplete domain coverage are at least partly acknowledged.
weaknesses: The central empirical support is not strong enough for the scale of the claims. The paper repeatedly emphasizes roughly 100B tasks, but this number is mostly combinatorial over a modest number of datasets/modules/backends and includes evaluation modes that are not actually studied. There is limited evidence that the vast generated space is meaningful, calibrated, non-redundant, or learnable beyond the selected DiscoBench subset.

The main evaluations do not convincingly validate DiscoGen as an optimization environment. The tested agents usually fail or underperform the all-fixed baseline, and the paper largely interprets this as evidence of task difficulty and room for improvement. That is useful diagnostically, but it does not show that the benchmark reliably drives better ADAs or that generated tasks provide a stable training signal.

The prompt-optimization result is suggestive but weak. The K_tasks trend in Table 4 has overlapping confidence intervals in several comparisons, appears to rely on a narrow prompt-tuning setup with one closed-source optimizer model, and does not appear to repeat the outer optimization process across seeds. The conclusion that performance improves with task diversity is therefore overstated.

The contamination-resistance claim is too strong. DiscoGen hides meta-test datasets during an agent run, but the paper publishes fixed DiscoBench splits and uses many public datasets and standard codebases. Once released, both the generator and benchmark can enter pretraining or retrieval corpora, and the proposed private API is future work rather than part of the evaluated contribution.

Reproducibility is mixed. The authors state that DiscoGen is open-source and provide many details, but the experiments require large compute, API-served models, and in one case a closed-source Claude prompt optimizer. The paper also uses future/model-version-specific systems and reports substantial development compute, making exact reproduction difficult for typical academic groups.

There are internal consistency and presentation issues that matter for a benchmark paper. For example, the On-Policy RL module count differs between Table 2/example configurations and the appendix description, and similar module-count ambiguity appears elsewhere. Such mismatches reduce confidence in the task-count derivations and implementation documentation.

The paper is long and often more aspirational than evidential. Section 6 proposes many exciting research directions, but these do not substitute for validation. The example discovered algorithms are hand-selected and anecdotal, so they do not establish that DiscoGen generally yields novel or useful algorithms.

The significance is potentially high if the released system is robust and adopted, but the current paper does not sufficiently demonstrate reliability, benchmark validity, or practical usefulness at the claimed scale. I would want stronger ablations, repeated ADA-optimization runs, clearer comparisons to existing benchmarks, consistency checks on generated tasks, and a more conservative treatment of the combinatorial task count before acceptance.

strengths: The paper tackles an important bottleneck for algorithm-discovery agents: scalable, controllable tasks with explicit meta-train/meta-test separation. The DiscoGen abstraction is well motivated and significantly more principled than evaluating agents on the same problems used during discovery.

The contribution is practically substantial: 14 domains, many editable modules/datasets/backends, a curated DiscoBench subset, task-count derivation, task lists, prompts, hyperparameters, cost/compute reporting, and planned open-source release give the work good reproducibility for a systems/benchmark paper.

The evaluation is broader than typical agent-benchmark papers. It measures multiple open-weight LLMs, single-edit and all-edit settings, success rates, Elo with confidence intervals, success@3/until-success analyses, prompt tuning, module-count difficulty sweeps, initialization ablations, and task redundancy via rank correlations.

The paper is honest about several limitations: contamination of a public DiscoBench, non-exhaustive domains, prompt tuning as only a limited ADA-optimization demonstration, high compute costs, and possible social/safety impacts of improving automated algorithm discovery.

Presentation is generally clear. The inner-loop/meta-loop/ADA-optimization terminology, task configuration example, and appendices make a complicated benchmark proposal understandable. The paper also does a good job connecting the benchmark design to concrete future research directions.
weaknesses: The central empirical demonstration that DiscoGen improves ADAs is still limited. The main ADA optimization experiment only tunes prompts for one scaffold/model family, over 30 updates, and the gains are modest with overlapping or near-overlapping confidence intervals in some held-out settings. This supports usefulness but not the stronger vision of broadly training better ADAs.

The large task-count claim is combinatorial and somewhat overstates semantic diversity. Many tasks share codebases, datasets, modules, and evaluation mechanics; the rank-correlation analysis helps, but it is based on a small set of agents and DiscoBench single-edit tasks rather than a direct validation of the full generated task distribution.

DiscoBench evaluation is useful but incomplete: only three open-source LLMs and one ReAct-style MLGym scaffold are tested, with three meta-seeds. Since many agents fail to beat the all-fixed baseline even when successful, the experiments show the benchmark has signal, but provide relatively little evidence that current ADAs discover consistently strong or novel algorithms.

The benchmark’s reproducibility depends on substantial infrastructure, API-served models, downloaded datasets, containers, and large compute. The paper reports details and costs, but independent reproduction of the full results will likely be expensive and brittle unless the released code includes strong caching, exact task manifests, model/version pinning, and runnable lightweight subsets.

The contamination mitigation is not fully solved. The authors recognize that a public DiscoBench can enter pretraining data and propose a future private API with hidden datasets, but the current paper’s evaluation benchmark will still face the same fixed-benchmark issue after release.

Some claims about safety and democratization are more aspirational than evidenced. The impact statement is thoughtful, but assertions that scoped algorithm discovery is safer than general automated science, or that DiscoGen democratizes the area, would need more concrete governance/access mechanisms and empirical support.
